headline: High: Copilot can write shared repo files while dbt-core reads warehouse data, creating default-path leakage and workflow corruption risks; prompt-injection is lower because no direct channel is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: dbt-core has no documented direct ingestion channel from GitHub Copilot, but Copilot can edit repo context/open buffers and dbt-core can operate on project files. That makes manual or file-based prompt injection plausible, though not default and with limited blast radius compared with direct tool bridges.
conditions: IF Copilot Workspace edits are copied into dbt project files that dbt-core later parses as instructions or macros, injection becomes possible.
IF a shared repo file is used as an instruction channel between the agents, the risk materializes.
mitigations: Keep Copilot suggestions out of dbt macro/config files unless reviewed.
Use separate branches for AI-generated edits and dbt execution.
Add a human review step before dbt parses any AI-authored file.
Restrict dbt runs to vetted directories only.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot reads repo context and open buffers and sends them to api.githubcopilot.com, while dbt-core touches data warehouse data and has allowlisted network egress. If warehouse-derived secrets or sensitive SQL land in shared files, Copilot can transmit them off-host by default; the pairwise path is plausible in normal use.
conditions: IF warehouse credentials, query results, or sensitive SQL are present in editor buffers or repo context, Copilot may transmit them to its backend.
IF dbt-core materializes sensitive data into files that Copilot can read, leakage occurs.
mitigations: Remove secrets and sensitive query outputs from repo files.
Disable Copilot on files containing warehouse credentials or sensitive SQL.
Use redacted fixtures for AI-assisted editing.
Separate dbt execution artifacts from editor-visible source files.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: dbt-core can call a data warehouse and Copilot can write filesystem edits in editor buffers; both can mutate shared project files or adjacent artifacts. Copilot’s edits are human-reviewed, but dbt-core may also generate or update warehouse-facing assets, so overlapping writes can conflict in default collaborative workflows.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repo files or generated artifacts in one session, write conflicts can occur.
IF dbt-generated files are committed while Copilot edits the same paths, git-state conflicts become possible.
mitigations: Use branch-per-agent workflows.
Lock generated directories during dbt runs.
Require one writer at a time for shared files.
Review and stage Copilot edits before dbt regeneration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot produces code and edits that a user may accept, while dbt-core executes warehouse transformations based on project files. If Copilot-authored changes are treated as authoritative and then run by dbt-core without validation, a bad suggestion can cascade into incorrect models or broken pipelines.
conditions: IF Copilot-generated SQL or model changes are accepted without review, dbt-core may execute them.
IF dbt-core consumes Copilot-edited project files as trusted inputs, downstream errors can propagate.
mitigations: Add tests before dbt execution.
Require code review for Copilot-authored changes.
Run dbt in dry-run or compile-only mode first.
Validate model diffs against expected schemas.

E_compliance.rationale: dbt-core touches data warehouse data, while Copilot sends editor/repo context to GitHub/Microsoft services. If regulated data or EU PII is present in the warehouse or repo, the pair can create a residency or retention mismatch; the profiles do not show a DPA or residency control, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF EU PII or regulated warehouse data appears in files or prompts sent to Copilot, cross-border processing may occur.
IF the organization requires a specific retention or residency policy for warehouse data, Copilot may violate it.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from Copilot-visible files.
Confirm a DPA and residency terms before use.
Mask sensitive identifiers in editor buffers.
Route regulated workloads to a separate workspace.
